Chapter 8. The Role of Intuition and the Unconscious Mind.
As you move deeper into any skill, something fascinating starts to happen. There’s a new kind of understanding—one that goes way beyond logic or step-by-step thinking.
Think about those moments when you’re in the middle of a competition. Decisions just seem to arrive in a split second—way too fast for you to consciously weigh every option. Maybe it’s a sudden move on the chessboard, a quick counter in the dojo, or the perfect phrase slipping into a conversation. These choices don’t feel calculated; they feel like instincts.
At first, it can feel almost mysterious, even a little unsettling. How does the right answer just appear out of nowhere, without you stopping to reason it out? You might remember a time in a high-pressure match, staring at a tangled, complex problem with barely any time left. Suddenly, a move pops into your mind—unexpected, yet somehow, it just makes sense. And only when you look back later do you realize how brilliant it actually was.
Here’s what’s really happening: intuition isn’t magic. It’s the outcome of deep, focused practice. Every hour you’ve spent studying patterns, repeating drills, or learning from your mistakes—all of that shapes your unconscious mind. Over time, your brain weaves together what you know and what you’ve experienced, letting insights bubble up right when you need them.
There’s a great story about a teacher who, after years and years of practice, just knows when a student is struggling—even if they haven’t said a word. Maybe it’s the way the student shifts in their seat, or a tiny flicker of hesitation. The teacher responds instantly, with empathy and support. That kind of knowing? You won’t find it in a manual. It grows from being present, caring, and really paying attention.
Most people actually underestimate intuition, thinking it’s unreliable or just guesswork. But in truth, it’s not an enemy of reason—it’s a powerful partner. The real secret is to trust the process: practice with intention, reflect honestly, and then—when the moment comes—let go and act. When your mind is quiet and your body’s prepared, intuition steps in to bridge the gap between what you know and how you perform.
And this doesn’t just show up in competition. Trusting your unconscious mind brings a sense of ease to everyday life, too. Choices start to feel more natural, your relationships grow deeper, and you find yourself more creative.
In the end, learning isn’t only about pushing forward—it’s also about listening inward, allowing your instincts and experience to guide you alongside your conscious efforts.
